deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page is in Add. MS a94 at Trinity College (the 'lost notebook' collection). The topic changes from the Hecke-type Euler products on the previous page to a modular-type transformation for the 'generalized eta product' P_s(q) = prod_{n>=1}(1 - q^{n^s}) with s a positive integer. The page header is (1-q^{1^s})(1-q^{2^s})(1-q^{3^s})...

MAIN CLAIM. Put q = e^{-2 pi x} with x > 0 and P(x) = prod_{n>=1}(1 - e^{-2 pi x n^s}). Then
(2 pi x)^{1/2} e^{pi x zeta(-s)} P(x) = (2 pi)^{s/2} exp( pi zeta(-1/s) / (x^{1/s} sin(pi/(2s))) ) * prod_{n in {1,3,...,2s-1}} prod_{lambda>=1} {1 - 2 e^{-2 pi (lambda/x)^{1/s} sin(pi n/(2s))} cos(2 pi (lambda/x)^{1/s} cos(pi n/(2s))) + e^{-4 pi (lambda/x)^{1/s} sin(pi n/(2s))}}^{1/2}.
The sign of the exponent is as I reconstruct it. The page may show a minus; see errors. The next page restates the formula with + pi zeta(-1/s)/(x^{1/s} sin).

DERIVATION (mine; the page gives only results). Two routes reach this.
(a) Mellin route. log P = -sum_{m,n} e^{-2 pi x m n^s}/m, whose Mellin transform is Gamma(w) zeta(w+1) zeta(sw) (2 pi x)^{-w}. Shifting the contour picks up three residues:
- w = 1/s gives Gamma(1+1/s) zeta(1+1/s) (2 pi x)^{-1/s}. By the functional equation this equals -pi zeta(-1/s)/(x^{1/s} sin(pi/(2s))).
- The double pole at w = 0 gives (1/2) log(2 pi x) - (s/2) log(2 pi), using zeta(0) = -1/2 and zeta'(0) = -(1/2) log 2 pi.
- w = -1 gives pi x zeta(-s).
These account exactly for the prefactors.
(b) Exact remainder. Use 1 - e^{-2 pi z} = 2 pi z e^{-pi z} prod_k (1 + z^2/k^2) with z = x n^s. Factor 1 + x^2 n^{2s}/k^2 over the 2s roots n = (k/x)^{1/s} e^{i pi j/(2s)}, j odd, and apply the sine product in n. Each root contributes |1 - exp(2 pi i r e^{i theta})|, with r = (lambda/x)^{1/s} and theta = pi j/(2s). This gives exactly the bracketed factor 1 - 2e^{-2 pi r sin theta} cos(2 pi r cos theta) + e^{-4 pi r sin theta}. The exponent 1/2 appears because j and 2s - j give identical factors.

SPECIAL CASES ON THE PAGE.
- s = 1: zeta(-1) = -1/12 and sin(pi/2) = 1. The cos factor is 1, so the bracket is (1 - e^{-2 pi lambda/x})^2. This gives sqrt(x) e^{-pi x/12} prod(1 - e^{-2 pi n x}) = e^{-pi/(12x)} prod(1 - e^{-2 pi n/x}). That is Dedekind's eta(i/x) = sqrt(x) eta(ix).
- s = 2: Ramanujan replaces x by x/2, so q = e^{-pi x}. Then zeta(-2) = 0, the angles pi/4 and 3pi/4 give equal factors, and sin(pi/4) = 1/sqrt2. The result is (1/2) sqrt(x/pi) e^{-2 pi zeta(-1/2)/sqrt x} prod(1 - e^{-pi n^2 x}) = prod_lambda {1 - 2 e^{-2 pi sqrt(lambda/x)} cos(2 pi sqrt(lambda/x)) + e^{-4 pi sqrt(lambda/x)}}.
- s = 3: zeta(-3) = 1/120 and sin(pi/6) = 1/2. The angles pi/6 and 5pi/6 give 1 - 2 e^{-pi r} cos(pi sqrt3 r) + e^{-2 pi r}, with r = (lambda/x)^{1/3}. The angle pi/2 gives (1 - e^{-2 pi r})^2, whose square root is 1 - e^{-2 pi r}. So sqrt(x) e^{pi x/120 - 2 pi zeta(-1/3)/x^{1/3}} prod(1 - e^{-2 pi x n^3}) = 2 pi prod_lambda (1 - e^{-2 pi r})(1 - 2e^{-pi r} cos(pi sqrt3 r) + e^{-2 pi r}). The factor 2 pi is (2 pi)^{3/2}/(2 pi)^{1/2}.

Purpose: an exact 'modular' transformation for generating functions related to partitions into s-th powers. It gives the asymptotic behaviour as q -> 1 together with an exponentially small, explicit error term. This connects to the Hardy–Ramanujan (1918) treatment of partitions into powers.
errors: General formula: the exponent on the right should be +pi*zeta(-1/s)/(x^{1/s} sin(pi/(2s))). The image appears to show e^{-pi zeta(-1/s)/...}. If so, this is a sign slip, since the s=1, 2 and 3 special cases on the same page, and the restatement on the next page, all use the correct sign. Note zeta(-1/s) < 0, so the correct sign makes P(x) -> 0 rapidly as x -> 0.

s=3 case: the factor coming from n = s (angle pi/2) should be (1 - e^{-2 pi (lambda/x)^{1/3}}), not (1 - e^{-pi (lambda/x)^{1/3}}) as it appears to be written. This is a slip, unless it is a misreading of the image.

The s=2 case silently rescales x -> x/2, so it uses q = e^{-pi x} rather than e^{-2 pi x}. The rescaling is done correctly: the prefactor (1/2)sqrt(x/pi) and the exponent 2 pi zeta(-1/2)/sqrt(x) are both right. My numerical check at x=1 gives about 0.9965 on both sides.
The s=1 case is correct: it is the eta transformation.
No derivation is given. The claim of an exact (not merely asymptotic) identity is justified only by my reconstruction (b), which supports it.

results.what: Exact transformation formula for prod_{n>=1}(1 - e^{-2 pi x n^s}), s a positive integer. It involves zeta(-s), zeta(-1/s), (2 pi)^{s/2}, and a double product over lambda and the odd 4s-th roots of unity in the upper half-plane.
results.modern_name: Modular-type transformation of the generalized Dedekind eta function prod(1-q^{n^N}). This is the exact refinement of the Hardy–Ramanujan / E. M. Wright asymptotics for partitions into s-th powers.
results.usually_credited_to: Asymptotics: Hardy & Ramanujan (1918) and E. M. Wright (1934). Exact explicit transformations of this type have been studied recently, e.g. Dixit, Kesarwani and Kumar (c. 2020–22), on generalized Lambert series and eta products.

results.what: Case s=1: sqrt(x) e^{-pi x/12} prod(1-e^{-2 pi n x}) = e^{-pi/(12x)} prod(1-e^{-2 pi n/x}).
results.modern_name: Dedekind eta transformation eta(-1/tau) = sqrt(-i tau) eta(tau)

results.what: Case s=2: transformation of prod(1-e^{-pi n^2 x}) into a product over lambda of 1 - 2e^{-2 pi sqrt(lambda/x)} cos(2 pi sqrt(lambda/x)) + e^{-4 pi sqrt(lambda/x)}, with factor e^{2 pi zeta(-1/2)/sqrt x}.
results.modern_name: Transformation of the 'square-eta' product prod(1-q^{n^2}), the generating function for partitions into distinct squares

results.what: Case s=3, with zeta(-3) = 1/120 and the factor 2 pi.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an exact, closed, modular-type transformation for prod(1-q^{n^s}), going beyond the leading-order asymptotics usually associated with partitions into powers. Such explicit formulas appear in the modern literature only recently. However, the page belongs to the lost-notebook material, which was published in facsimile in 1988, and the method is elementary (Mellin transform or partial fractions). It may therefore already be documented by Andrews–Berndt or by Dixit and coauthors; I am not sure. Overall it is a notable but not revolutionary detail.
